notes: \cpara{Opens with a joke: a question from an imagined reader who wants to be seen as generous without spending much.}

\cpara{Reports Hsee's gift result. The sentence leaves out what made it work. Respondents were told the store's price range: scarves from \$5 to \$50, coats from \$50 to \$500. The \$45 scarf sat near the top of its range and the \$55 coat near the bottom (as described by Vonasch et al., \textsc{Collabra: Psychology}, 2023, who replicated the study). The post states the general rule, the cheaper the class the more expensive an item looks, only near its end.}
\cpara{Introduces Hsee's 1996 dictionary study. Respondents were students asked to imagine they were music majors in a used bookstore, planning to spend \$10 to \$50.}

\clogic{Hsee's gift study had no side-by-side condition, so it did not show the reversal that the dictionaries show. The 2023 replication added one: 63\% of those shown both gifts chose the scarf. The replicators say this may mean the cheapest coat is seen as a poor coat, in which case the paradigm would not show a reversal at all; they could not settle the question.}

\cpara{The figures match Hsee's Figure 1, with about 39 respondents in each group. In joint evaluation B was worth more by a wide margin. In separate evaluation the gap for A (\$24 against \$20) was not significant on its own ($p = .1$); what was significant was the reversal, the difference between the two gaps ($p < .001$).}

\cpara{Gives Hsee's explanation: a number of entries means little on its own, while a torn cover is plainly bad. Slovic and colleagues, the post's next source, put it in the same affective terms: the defect is ``an affective variable.''}
\cpara{Completes the explanation: side by side, the entries can be compared, and they then outweigh the cover.}
\cpara{Turns to gambles, from Slovic and colleagues.}

\cfact{Most of the gamble figures that follow (the prices, the 13.2 and 7.5, the 33\% and 60.8\%, ``exceeded our expectations'') are in another paper by the same authors, ``The Affect Heuristic'' (2002; reprinted 2007). ``Rational Actors or Rational Fools'' gives only the 9.4 and 14.9.}

\cpara{The figures and the procedure match ``The Affect Heuristic'': subjects were told a pair of bets would be selected and they would play the one rated or priced higher, and some gambles were in fact played.}
\cpara{Gives the researchers' hypothesis, compatibility between the response scale and the part of the gamble, as the source states it.}
\cpara{Describes the added 5-cent loss and why it should make the \$9 easier to value.}
\cpara{Matches the source. It also reports that a gamble with a 25-cent loss (mean 11.7) was still rated above the gamble with no loss.}

\cpara{Matches the source: 96 University of Oregon students, split between the two gambles. Both gambles are worth less on average than the sure \$2: $\frac{7}{36} \times 9 = 1.75$ dollars, and about 1.71 with the loss. So 60.8\% chose a gamble worth less than the sum they gave up.}
\cpara{States the moral, correctly: the new gamble is strictly worse than the old one. Ends with an aside about designing AI.}
\cpara{Stated as a fact. The source reports no test in which both gambles were shown together. It is a reasonable prediction from the dictionary results, not a finding.}

\cpara{The text does not say what the figure shows. Vendor H serves 8 oz of ice cream in a 10 oz cup; Vendor L serves 7 oz overfilling a 5 oz cup (Hsee 1998, as described in the 2023 replication's materials). Without the image a reader cannot tell that H gives more ice cream.}

\cpara{The figures match those reported for Hsee's study. Hsee did not give group sizes; the 2023 replicators assume about 23 per group. Their replication found the same pattern with a smaller effect in separate evaluation.}
\cpara{Applies the result to gifts: a \$400 iPod Touch is the top of its class, a \$400 Wii the bottom of its class, and the recipient sees only one.}

\cpara{The advice, offered as a joke with a true core. Its rule, ``The cheaper the class of objects, the more expensive a particular object will appear,'' is Hsee's own conclusion from the scarf study. It works only if the recipient knows roughly what the class costs, as Hsee's respondents were told.}
\cpara{Extends the joke to Japanese gift melons, and then to \$25 toothpicks and \$10 dust specks.}
\cpara{A closing joke.}
